148.title: The unbroken reading
148.hook: the whole Granth read aloud without a break, taking about forty-eight hours
148.howItsDone: For gurpurabs, family occasions and times of grief or thanks, Sikhs hold an akhand path: a team of readers takes turns to read the whole Guru Granth Sahib aloud without a break, over about forty-eight hours, ending with the bhog.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Nanak's gurpurab, lamps on the full moon of Katak. Your line was the light that came. Who did you think of when you switched on a light? Day one hundred forty-eight.

It's three in the morning in a gurdwara. The hall is almost empty. The lights are low. Outside, the city is asleep. But at the front, one person is sitting behind the Guru Granth Sahib, reading aloud, steadily, page after page. A few people sit wrapped in shawls, listening. In an hour or two, someone else will slide in beside the reader, pick up the line mid-sentence, and carry on, without a single second of silence in between. It started two days ago. It won't stop until the last page.
screen: `3 A.M., THE HALL NEARLY EMPTY.` → `ONE VOICE, READING ON.` → `NOT A SECOND OF SILENCE.`

segments.voice: It's an akhand path. Akhand means unbroken, undivided. Path means reading, recitation. So it's the unbroken reading: the whole Guru Granth Sahib, all 1,430 angs, read aloud from beginning to end without any break. It takes about forty-eight hours. No one person can do it alone, so a team of readers, called pathis, take turns, usually in shifts of about two hours. When one reader's time is up, the next sits beside them and takes over the words mid-flow, so the reading is never interrupted. Families and gurdwaras hold an akhand path for the big moments: gurpurabs, as you heard yesterday, and Vaisakhi, but also a wedding, a new baby, a new house, a death in the family, or simply to give thanks. It begins with Ardas and karah prashad. It ends with the bhog, the completion: the last pages are read, then Anand Sahib, Ardas, a hukamnama and prashad, often followed by langar. Nobody is expected to listen to all forty-eight hours. People drop in, sit for a while, leave, come back. Some stay up through the night to keep the readers company. What matters is that the word keeps sounding, through the day and the dark, unbroken. There's another way too: a sahaj path, a steady reading of the whole Granth at your own pace, over weeks or months. Many families do this at home. Both come from the same wish: to hear the whole of the Guru's word, from Japji at the start to the last page, in order, all the way through.
screen: `AKHAND — UNBROKEN. PATH — READING.` · `1,430 ANGS, ABOUT 48 HOURS.` · `READERS TAKE TURNS MID-LINE.` · `THE BHOG, THE COMPLETION.` · then, large: `UNBROKEN.`

segments.voice: Today, find a recording of Gurbani being read, a path, and give it ten minutes at some point: on a walk, while cooking, before sleep. For now, begin with these two minutes. Play it if you can, or just sit. Imagine yourself at three in the morning in that nearly empty hall, wrapped in a shawl, listening to a voice that hasn't stopped for a day and a half. You don't need to understand. Just keep it company. The bell holds the time.
Akhand path. The unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, about forty-eight hours, readers taking turns so the word never stops.
Your line: unbroken. Today, choose one small thing to keep going all day, a kindness, a patience, a word under the breath, and see if you can leave it unbroken until bed. Day one hundred forty-eight.

149.title: Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab
149.hook: his birth is celebrated in winter with kirtan and processions
149.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab in December or January with an akhand path, nagar kirtan, kirtan and langar; large gatherings are held at Takht Sri Patna Sahib, his birthplace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the akhand path, the unbroken reading. Your line was unbroken. What did you manage to keep going all day? Today, another gurpurab, in the middle of winter. Day one hundred forty-nine.

Think of someone you know who seems to hold two opposite things in one person. The nurse who's gentle with patients and fierce with bad doctors. The grandmother who writes poetry and once faced down a landlord. We tend to sort people into boxes: the soft ones, the tough ones. The tenth Guru doesn't fit in either box. He wrote some of the most beautiful devotional poetry in Sikh prayer, and he led armies. Sikhs celebrate his birthday in the heart of winter. Today, Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab.
screen: `GENTLE AND FIERCE AT ONCE.` → `POET AND COMMANDER.` → `A BIRTHDAY IN WINTER.`

segments.voice: Guru Gobind Singh was born in 1666 in Patna, in eastern India, where a great gurdwara, one of the five Takhts, the seats of Sikh authority, now stands. His gurpurab falls in December or January, and it's kept the way you'd now expect: an akhand path, a nagar kirtan through the streets, kirtan and langar, and at Patna Sahib, pilgrims by the thousand. The exact date moves from year to year, and different Sikh calendars have calculated it differently; Sikhs have debated that, but not the celebration itself. Now the sword and the song. You've already met his words on this path: Jaap Sahib's galloping praise, the savaiyas that say without love, nothing, Chaupai asking to be kept under God's hand. He was a poet in several languages and kept poets at his court. And he was also a military leader who fought many battles to defend his people, created the Khalsa, and lost his father and all four of his sons in those years of persecution. How do the two fit? Sikhs call the ideal sant sipahi: saint-soldier. Devotion first, and courage in its service. In a Persian letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh says, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Every other means first. And then there's a line of his that many Sikhs love. In paraphrase: recognize the whole human race as one. That's the song the sword was meant to protect.
screen: `BORN IN PATNA, 1666.` · `A WINTER GURPURAB.` · `SANT SIPAHI — SAINT-SOLDIER.` · `THE WHOLE HUMAN RACE AS ONE.` · then, large: `SWORD AND SONG.`

segments.voice: Read one line of his. Here's the one to hold: recognize the whole human race as one. Say it silently, slowly, three times. Then think of one group of people you find hard to see as your own, whoever it is for you. Just hold them in the line for a few breaths. Not agreeing with everything. Just human, one kind with you. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab. The tenth Guru's birthday, kept in winter with kirtan and processions: the poet-commander, sword and song.
Your line: sword and song. Today, be gentle where you'd usually be hard, and brave where you'd usually go quiet, once each. Day one hundred forty-nine.

150.title: Guru Arjan's martyrdom day
150.hook: in the June heat Sikhs hand out cold sweetened water to passers-by
150.howItsDone: On and around the anniversary of Guru Arjan's martyrdom in June, Sikhs set up chhabeels, stalls handing out chilled sweetened drinks free to passers-by, alongside kirtan and prayers at the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab, the poet and commander. Your line was sword and song. Where were you gentle, and where were you brave? Today, a harder day in the Sikh year, and a surprising way to keep it. Day one hundred fifty.
screen: `GURU GOBIND SINGH'S GURPURAB — SWORD AND SONG.`

segments.voice: The night before, somebody's garage fills up with bags of ice. Big steel drums get rinsed out with a hose. There's a crate of milk, a sack of sugar, maybe a bottle of rose syrup, and a stack of paper cups as tall as a child. By mid-morning there's a table at a busy corner, it's well over a hundred degrees, and a line of teenagers is standing in the traffic with trays, waving cars down. On day sixty-four, you were the driver being handed a cup. Today, step around to the other side of the table.
screen: `ICE AND STEEL DRUMS, THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `TRAYS HELD OUT INTO THE TRAFFIC.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: The stall is called a chhabeel. The word is usually traced to the Arabic sabil, a public water fountain given as charity, the kind built in Muslim cities from Cairo to Istanbul; a free drink of water is honored on more than one path. You already know whose day it is. On days sixty-three and sixty-four you met Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, held in Lahore in the summer of 1606, the first Sikh shaheed, and the line he held to: your will is sweet. Today isn't the story again. It's how the Sikh year keeps it. The anniversary falls in the hottest weeks, in May or June, depending on which calendar a gurdwara follows. Inside, there is kirtan of his hymns and an Ardas. Outside, the chhabeel. Here is how one actually runs. The drink is often kachi lassi: water with a little milk and sugar, sometimes rose syrup, poured over ice in those steel drums. It's handed out with both hands, to anyone, without asking a name or a faith. Truck drivers, police officers, schoolkids, strangers. A good chhabeel ends up with more helpers than it planned, because people walking past stop to pour. Some run for an afternoon, some for a week. Notice who holds the trays: very often the young. That's how a memory four hundred years old gets handed on. Not as a lecture about cruelty, but as a job: standing in the heat, cooling someone else.
screen: `CHHABEEL — FROM SABIL, A FREE FOUNTAIN.` · `GURU ARJAN'S DAY, IN THE HEAT.` · `KACHI LASSI, ICE AND BOTH HANDS.` · `A MEMORY HANDED ON AS A JOB.` · then, large: `COOL WATER FOR ANYONE.`

segments.voice: Give someone a cold drink, today if you can. For now, get yourself a glass of cool water, if one's near, and hold it. Feel the cold in your hands. Take one slow sip. Think of someone who's worn out, overheated, overworked today: a delivery driver, a coworker, someone at home. Picture handing them this glass, and their face as they take it. If you pray, you can remember Guru Arjan's calm. The bell holds the time.
Chhabeel. A stall of cold sweetened drinks given free to passers-by, remembering Guru Arjan, who was martyred in the heat.
Your line: cool water for anyone. Today, hand someone a cold drink, a delivery driver, a neighbor, a stranger, and ask nothing back. Day one hundred fifty.

151.title: Bandi Chhor Divas
151.hook: lamps are lit to remember Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior, at Diwali time
151.howItsDone: On Bandi Chhor Divas, which falls at Diwali time, Sikhs light lamps and candles at home and in gurdwaras; the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is illuminated and fireworks are set off over its pool.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan's martyrdom day, and a cup of cold water on a hot road. Your line was cool water for anyone. Did someone get a drink from you, or did you at least notice who might need one? Day one hundred fifty-one.

Autumn, and across much of India the lamps come out. Diwali: rows of little clay lamps on windowsills, fireworks, boxes of sweets passed over walls to the neighbors. Hindus light them for Rama coming home, and for Lakshmi. Jains light them for Mahavira. And in Amritsar, on the same nights, the Golden Temple is outlined in light and doubled in its pool, with fireworks over the water that people travel a long way to see. Sikhs are lighting lamps too, for a story of their own. It's about a prison, a Guru who wouldn't leave alone, and a cloak.
screen: `LAMPS ON EVERY WINDOWSILL.` → `THE GOLDEN TEMPLE, DOUBLED IN ITS POOL.` → `A PRISON, AND A CLOAK.`

segments.voice: The day is called Bandi Chhor Divas. Bandi means a prisoner. Chhor is the one who releases. Divas is day. The day of the one who freed the prisoners. Here's the story as Sikhs tell it. Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, was held by the Mughal emperor Jahangir in the fort at Gwalior. Historians argue about how long he was there and exactly why; the sources don't settle it. Tradition says that inside the fort he met other prisoners, fifty-two rajas, local kings held there for reasons of politics. When the emperor finally ordered the Guru's release, the Guru refused to walk out alone. He asked that the rajas go free with him. The emperor, the story goes, answered with a condition meant to sound like a no: as many as can hold on to your cloak may leave. So the Guru had a cloak made with fifty-two long tassels, one for each raja. Each of them took hold of one, and they all walked out through the gate together. That's why Sikhs call him Bandi Chhor, the liberator. Sikhs remember that when he reached Amritsar, people lit lamps to welcome him, and it was Diwali time. Sikhs have lit lamps for it ever since. Notice what the story is proud of. Not an escape. A refusal to be free alone. The Guru's own release was a door, and he held it open until everyone behind him was through. Sikhs and Hindus lighting lamps on the same nights, each for their own reasons, side by side, is one of the ordinary beauties of Punjab.
screen: `BANDI — PRISONER. CHHOR — RELEASER.` · `FIFTY-TWO RAJAS IN THE FORT.` · `A CLOAK WITH FIFTY-TWO TASSELS.` · `NOT FREE ALONE.` · then, large: `BANDI CHHOR.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is a lamp. If there's a candle or a tea light nearby, and it's safe, light it now. If not, picture one: small, steady, a little flicker at the top. Then think of someone who got free of something. Out of a hospital. Out of a bad job, a hard year, a debt, a cell. Hold them in that light for a while. If someone you know is still waiting to get free, hold them too, right beside the first. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
Bandi Chhor. The liberator of prisoners: a name for Guru Hargobind, who would not leave the fort at Gwalior without the fifty-two.
Your line: light for the freed. Sometime today, when you're let out of something, a meeting, a long line, a waiting room, hold the door for whoever is behind you. Day one hundred fifty-one.

152.title: Hola Mohalla
152.hook: at Anandpur, the day after Holi, mock battles, gatka and poetry fill the fields
152.howItsDone: At Hola Mohalla, held at Anandpur Sahib the day after Holi, Sikhs gather for about three days of gatka, horsemanship, kirtan, poetry and langar, ending with a large procession; Nihang Singhs lead many of the martial displays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bandi Chhor: a Guru who wouldn't leave the fort without the fifty-two. Your line was light for the freed. Did you hold a door for anyone? Day one hundred fifty-two.

Picture a wide field in March. The day before, much of north India played Holi: colored powder everywhere, everyone pink and green and laughing. The next morning, at Anandpur Sahib in Punjab, something else begins. Horses thunder across the open ground. A rider in a tall blue turban stands up on two galloping horses at once. Pairs face off with sticks and small shields, spinning, blocking, grinning. Somewhere a poet is reciting to a crowd. Somewhere else a langar is feeding thousands. It's loud and dusty and joyful. It's Hola Mohalla.
screen: `HOLI, THE DAY BEFORE.` → `HORSES, STICKS AND SHIELDS.` → `A POET, A LANGAR, A CROWD.`

segments.voice: Hola Mohalla goes back to Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says that around 1701, at Anandpur, he called the Sikhs together the day after Holi, not for colored powder but for drills and mock battles. People explain the name in more than one way. Hola is often linked to Holi, and also to halla, a charge. Mohalla is usually taken as an organized column, like a company on the march. Either way the picture is the same: a festival of movement. Why would a Guru do that? Remember the times. Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur had both been executed. The Khalsa had been founded just a couple of years before. Guru Gobind Singh wanted a people who could defend themselves and others, and who weren't ruled by fear. So he took a season of play and pointed it at courage and skill. The play stayed. It's still a game and still a joy, but it trains the body. Today the festival runs for about three days. There's gatka, the Sikh art of stick and sword. There's horsemanship, much of it from the Nihang Singhs, in deep blue, who keep the old martial ways alive. There's kirtan, and there are gatherings of poets; Guru Gobind Singh kept poets at his court. And it closes with a great procession. Underneath is an idea you've met before: the saint-soldier. Devotion and strength aren't opposites. A body that can run, stand and protect belongs to a life given to the Name. Strength, in joy, not in anger.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER HOLI, AT ANANDPUR.` · `HOLA — A CHARGE. MOHALLA — A COLUMN.` · `PLAY, POINTED AT COURAGE.` · `GATKA, HORSES AND POETRY.` · then, large: `THE SAINT-SOLDIER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice moves. Stand up if you can. Roll your shoulders back. Shake out your hands. March gently in place, or step side to side. If you're sitting, lift your arms and sweep them slowly, like you're parting tall grass. Keep it light: this is a festival, not a workout. Let your breath keep time with your body. If you pray, let Waheguru ride on the breath. Notice the strength you have today, however much or little it is, and enjoy it. Then slow down, and let the body settle. The bell holds the time.
Hola Mohalla. The festival of mock battles, gatka and poetry at Anandpur, the day after Holi, begun by Guru Gobind Singh.

Your line: strength, in joy. Use your body for something today and let yourself enjoy it: the stairs, a fast walk, carrying the groceries in one trip. Strong and glad at the same time. Day one hundred fifty-two.

153.title: Maghi at Muktsar
153.hook: the fair at Muktsar in January remembers the Forty Liberated
153.howItsDone: On Maghi, in mid-January, Sikhs gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib for a large fair, bathe in the sacred pool, and remember the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated, with kirtan, prayers and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hola Mohalla: horses, gatka and poetry the day after Holi. Your line was strength, in joy. Did your body get to do something glad? Day one hundred fifty-three.

Most of us know someone who walked away and then came back. The friend who went quiet for a year and finally texted: sorry. The brother who left home angry and turned up one Thanksgiving. Maybe it was you. Coming back is hard, because you have to walk in past everything you said on the way out. Every January, in a town in Punjab called Sri Muktsar Sahib, a huge fair fills the streets, and at its heart is a story about forty men who did exactly that.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO WENT QUIET.` → `WALKING BACK IN.` → `FORTY MEN WHO CAME BACK.`

segments.voice: The fair is called Maghi, because it falls on the first day of Magh, a winter month in the Punjabi calendar, usually in mid-January. The story goes back to the early 1700s. Guru Gobind Singh and his Sikhs had been under siege at Anandpur for months, and food had run out. Tradition says a group of about forty Sikhs from the Majha region decided they'd had enough. The Guru let them go, but asked them to put it in writing: a note saying, in effect, you are not our Guru, and we are not your Sikhs. They signed it and went home. At home they weren't welcomed as heroes. Tradition remembers a woman, Mai Bhago, also called Mata Bhag Kaur, who shamed them for leaving, and then rode back with them herself. They caught up with the Guru's small band near a lake called Khidrana, just as Mughal troops closed in. The forty stood and fought, and they fell. Afterward, the Guru walked among the fallen. One of them, Mahan Singh, was still barely alive. He asked for one thing: tear up the note. Tradition says the Guru took it from his clothes, tore it in front of him, and Mahan Singh died at peace. The Guru called them the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated, and the place became Muktsar, the pool of liberation. Look at what the story honors. Not people who never left. People who left, and came back anyway. And a Guru who had kept the note close all along, so it could be torn.
screen: `MAGHI — THE FIRST DAY OF MAGH.` · `FORTY SIGN A NOTE AND LEAVE.` · `MAI BHAGO LEADS THEM BACK.` · `THE NOTE, TORN UP.` · then, large: `CHALI MUKTE — THE FORTY LIBERATED.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and think of someone who came back. A friend who returned after a silence. A relative who made it home. Someone who came back to health, or to sobriety, or to their faith, or to you. Picture their face at the moment they walked back in, and notice what it cost them. Now, if you're willing, think of one place you left that you might one day return to. You don't have to go. Just look at the door. If you pray, you can hold both of them in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Maghi. The first day of the winter month of Magh, when the fair at Muktsar remembers the Forty Liberated.

Your line: come back, anyway. Today, send one small message to someone you drifted away from. Two words is plenty. Or, if someone comes back to you, let them in without the speech. Day one hundred fifty-three.

154.title: Shaheedi Jor Mela
154.hook: in December Sikhs gather at Fatehgarh Sahib to remember the younger Sahibzade
154.howItsDone: In late December, Sikhs gather at Fatehgarh Sahib for the Shaheedi Jor Mela with kirtan, prayers, langar and a procession; many families observe the week in mourning, sleeping on the floor and keeping celebrations away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maghi, and the Forty Liberated who came back. Your line was come back, anyway. Did you send that small message, or at least look at the door? Day one hundred fifty-four.

In the last week of December, while much of the world is between holidays, the roads around a town in Punjab called Fatehgarh Sahib fill with people. Huge crowds come. There's langar along the roadsides, kirtan in tents, a long, slow procession. But it isn't a celebration. Many families have spent the week sleeping on the floor instead of in their beds. Some give up sweets. The mood is quiet. They've come to remember two little boys and their grandmother.
screen: `A TOWN FULL OF PEOPLE IN DECEMBER.` → `NOT A CELEBRATION.` → `TWO BOYS AND THEIR GRANDMOTHER.`

segments.voice: The gathering is the Shaheedi Jor Mela. Shaheedi means of the martyrs. Jor mela is a gathering, a coming together. Here is what Sikhs remember. In December of 1704, Guru Gobind Singh's household left the fort at Anandpur after a long siege. At a flooded river, the Sarsa, in the dark and the chaos, the family was separated. The Guru's mother, Mata Gujri, went on with her two youngest grandsons: Zorawar Singh, about nine, and Fateh Singh, about six. A former servant, Gangu, took them in and then, tradition says, gave them up to the authorities. They were brought to Sirhind, to the Mughal governor, Wazir Khan. The boys were offered their lives if they would give up their faith. They refused. Tradition says they were ordered to be bricked into a wall, and they were put to death there. Mata Gujri died in the cold tower where they had been held. Two more details matter to Sikhs as much as the grief. The Nawab of Malerkotla, Sher Muhammad Khan, a Muslim, protested in open court that children must not be punished, and Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since. And a merchant named Todar Mal, tradition says, bought the ground for their cremation by covering it with gold coins. The town is now called Fatehgarh, after the younger boy. People sometimes say the boys were too young to understand what they were choosing. Sikhs remember it the other way: small, and yet they would not bend.
screen: `SHAHEEDI — OF THE MARTYRS.` · `SEPARATED AT THE SARSA RIVER.` · `TWO BOYS WHO WOULD NOT BEND.` · `MALERKOTLA SPOKE UP.` · then, large: `THE YOUNGER SAHIBZADE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is quiet. No doing. Sit still, and think of the two boys and their grandmother. You don't need to picture the wall. Picture them together, her hand resting on each small head. Then let the circle widen to children anywhere who are carrying things too heavy for them. If you pray, you can hold them all in Waheguru. If you don't, simply keep them company in the silence, the way you'd sit beside someone who is grieving. The bell holds the time.
Shaheedi Jor Mela. The gathering at Fatehgarh Sahib each December to remember the younger Sahibzade and Mata Gujri.

Your line: small, and unbending. Today, notice a child's courage: saying sorry first, trying again, telling the truth when it costs. And look back at this week: an unbroken reading, a Guru's birthday, cool water, lamps for the freed, strength in joy, and coming back. Day one hundred fifty-four.

screen: `DAY 154 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: GURU TEGH BAHADUR'S MARTYRDOM DAY.`
